newsitem.title: UK: German politician sees Eurofighter go-ahead.
newsitem.headline: German politician sees Eurofighter go-ahead.

text.p: A senior German opposition politician said on Wednesday he was confident his country would give the go-ahead to the four-nation Eurofighter despite internal wrangling in Bonn that has threatened the project.

Walter Kolbow, defence policy spokesman for the Social Democrats, said he had been assured by ministers that the German government would come up with an acceptable means of funding its share of the project.
"The government must say how they will finance it," he told BBC radio. "Then we will decide."

Continued German participation in the Eurofighter has been threatened by the country's financial crisis as it attempts to make spending cuts in order to qualify for the planned single European currency.
"I think it will go ahead," Kolbow said. "They will have a solution to finance this aircraft."
Britain hopes Germany can overcome the problems which have hampered development of the Eurofighter, a project which holds the key to thousands of British jobs.

British Defence Secretary George Robertson is due to meet his counterpart Volker Ruehe in Germany on Wednesday ahead of talks on Friday between Prime Minister Tony Blair and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
A deal could be struck in time for the Blair-Kohl talks and defence sources said they hoped a statement would be issued after Robertson meets Ruehe.
Ruehe said on Sunday he was confident that Bonn would find the funds needed to buy 180 Eurofighters to replace its ageing Phantom jets and modernise its air force.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has proposed redirecting state aid for the Airbus airliner to the Eurofighter project to help toward the planned 23 billion mark ($13.3 billion) purchase.
Ruehe has already offered to provide one billion marks from his own budget and if Waigel comes up with another billion, production of the jet can start.
Eurofighter, developed jointly by Germany, Britain, Italy and Spain, is designed to be the next generation of fighter jet.
But Britain has warned that the dispute between Germany's defence and finance ministries over whether to go ahead with the purchase is increasing doubts about Eurofighter's viability.
In particular, delays to the project could hit export hopes at a time when both the United Arab Emirates and Norway have shortlisted Eurofighter for their air forces.
Robertson told parliament in a written answer on Monday that Eurofighter already sustained 6,000 jobs in Britain -- a figure which was expected to rise to 14,000 at the peak of production.
Media reports have suggested Britain will encourage Germany to go ahead with Eurofighter by signing up to the European Future Large Aircraft (FLA) programme.
The FLA is designed to provide a home grown European alternative to the C130J Hercules produced by Lockheed Martin of the United States.
Robertson said on Monday the FLA was "a potential solution to our future air transport requirements".

Eurofighter is being developed by a consortium made up of British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain and Finmeccanica of Italy's Alenia. ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
